technique.how: Seat the patient so that lying back will leave the head hanging ~20 degrees below the table edge; turn the head 45 degrees toward the tested ear, then move briskly to supine with head extended and eyes open. Observe for 30-60 s for latency, nystagmus direction, duration, and vertigo; sit up and test the other side.
technique.prerequisites: Positional history (brief vertigo on rolling over, lying down, looking up); patient able to lie flat with neck extension; explain that vertigo may be provoked.
technique.contraindications: Cervical spine instability or severe cervical stenosis, recent neck surgery, carotid dissection concern, or inability to tolerate the position; use the side-lying test instead.

interpretation.positive_finding: After a latency of seconds, upbeating torsional nystagmus toward the lower ear with vertigo, lasting under 60 s and fatiguing on repetition, is diagnostic of posterior-canal BPPV on that side.
interpretation.negative_finding: A negative test does not exclude BPPV (single-study sensitivity about 79%); repeat the maneuver, check for horizontal canal BPPV with the supine roll test, or re-test another day.
interpretation.pitfalls: Persistent, non-fatiguing, purely vertical (downbeat) or direction-changing positional nystagmus without latency suggests a central positional lesion, not BPPV. Nystagmus is easy to miss without removing fixation or with tentative positioning.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: treat with Epley repositioning at the bedside, no imaging needed if otherwise typical. Atypical nystagmus or persistent symptoms: pursue central causes.

estimates.population: 61 patients referred with positional vertigo to a tertiary vestibular diagnostic laboratory (Cohen 2004), appraised in a structured critically appraised topic
estimates.reference_standard: No independent standard; Dix-Hallpike compared with side-lying test response (nystagmus slow-phase velocity) in the same patients
estimates.quote: sensitivity was 79% [95% confidence interval (CI) 65-94], specificity was 75% (33-100), positive likelihood ratio (LR) was 3.17 (95% CI 0.58-17.50), negative LR was 0.28
estimates.location: Abstract, Results (CAT estimates derived from Cohen 2004)

estimates.target_condition: BPPV of any canal (traditional bedside Dix-Hallpike plus supine roll testing)
estimates.population: 201 participants aged >=60 with suspected BPPV, randomized crossover
estimates.reference_standard: Mechanical rotation chair diagnostics (Dix-Hallpike and supine roll tests in the chair)
estimates.computed_from: LRs computed from abstract sens 0.79 and spec 0.95: LR+ = 0.79/0.05 = 15.8; LR- = 0.21/0.95 = 0.22. Prevalence = 68/201 (chair diagnosis). Sensitivity for non-posterior BPPV was 0.63 and fell to 0.60 with impaired cooperation.
estimates.quote: TB diagnostics demonstrated a sensitivity of 79%, specificity of 95%, PPV of 89%, and NPV of 90%

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not perform in patients with spontaneous nystagmus at rest (acute vestibular syndrome) as a substitute for HINTS/gait assessment, or when neck extension is unsafe.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Positional nystagmus that is downbeating, direction-changing, non-fatiguing, or without latency, or any positional vertigo with other neurological signs, needs MRI for a central positional lesion.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Bedside versus mechanical-chair diagnosis agreed with kappa 0.76 in elderly patients (Hougaard 2026); sensitivity falls with poor patient cooperation or hesitant positioning.

extraction_notes: The classic Dix-Hallpike accuracy figures (79%/75%) come from a critically appraised topic (Halker 2008, kind recorded as meta_analysis because it is a structured evidence appraisal) that identified a single weak primary study (Cohen 2004, PMID 15021771, cited separately; its abstract reports no sens/spec). Wide CIs and absence of an independent reference standard limit these numbers. The 2026 Danish study measures bedside DH plus supine roll against a rotation-chair standard in the elderly, so it is entered as a separate estimate. AAO-HNS 2017 guideline defines the positive test (torsional upbeating nystagmus with the affected ear down).
